summary: Describes RTP, a protocol for carrying real-time data such as audio and video over unicast or multicast networks. It adds sequencing and timing information so receivers can play media back smoothly, and it comes with a companion control protocol. It was replaced by RFC 3550.

plainLanguage.summary: When you watch a live video, the pieces must arrive in order and on time. This protocol puts a number and a clock reading on each piece so the player can put them back together smoothly.

questions: how does real-time audio and video transport work
how big is the rtp header
what is an ssrc in rtp
subtitle: The original specification of RTP and its control protocol RTCP, built to carry live audio and video over IP.

tldr.problem: Live audio and video need to know the order, timing and payload type of each packet, plus feedback on how well delivery is going, but the network guarantees none of that.
tldr.mechanism: RTP adds a 12-byte header with a sequence number, a timestamp, a payload type and a source identifier. A companion control protocol, RTCP, carries reception reports and participant identification, with its traffic kept to a small share of session bandwidth.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1889 has been replaced by RFC 3550. RTP itself offers no delivery or quality-of-service guarantee.

today: RFC 1889 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3550, which is now the specification of RTP and RTCP.

sections.title: What RTP Provides and What It Does Not
sections.content:
The real-time transport protocol (RTP) provides end-to-end delivery services for data with real-time characteristics, such as interactive audio and video. Those services include payload type identification, sequence numbering, timestamping and delivery monitoring. Applications typically run RTP on top of UDP, and RTP supports multicast distribution if the underlying network provides it.

RTP does not provide any mechanism to ensure timely delivery or other quality-of-service guarantees. It does not guarantee delivery or prevent out-of-order delivery. The sequence numbers let the receiver reconstruct the sender's order.

The document defines two closely linked parts: RTP, which carries the data, and the RTP control protocol (RTCP), which monitors quality of service and conveys information about participants. RTP is a deliberately incomplete framework. A full specification for an application also needs a profile, which defines payload type codes and their mapping to payload formats, and payload format documents for each encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP is like numbering and time-stamping the pages of a flip book as you mail them. It cannot make the post office faster, but the receiver can put the pages in order.

sections.title: Sessions, Sources, Mixers and Translators
sections.content:
An RTP session is the association among participants, defined by a pair of destination transport addresses (one network address plus a port pair for RTP and RTCP). Each medium in a multimedia conference is carried in its own session, so audio and video use different port pairs or multicast addresses. This lets a participant receive only one medium if they choose.

A synchronization source (SSRC) is the source of a stream of RTP packets, identified by a randomly chosen 32-bit SSRC identifier rather than a network address. A contributing source (CSRC) is a source that contributed to a stream combined by a mixer.

Two kinds of relay sit between end systems. A mixer combines streams into a new one, possibly changing the encoding, and becomes the synchronization source of its output. A translator forwards packets with their SSRC identifier intact, for example to convert encodings, replicate from multicast to unicast, or filter through a firewall. Both can be used to serve a participant on a low-bandwidth link or behind a firewall.
sections.plainLanguage: Each speaker gets a random name tag. A mixer is like a person who blends several voices into one recording. A translator is like a courier who passes each message along unchanged.

sections.title: The RTP Data Header
sections.content:
Every RTP packet starts with a fixed header of twelve octets. A list of CSRC identifiers follows only when a mixer inserts one. The fixed fields are:

  • V (2 bits): the version, which is 2.
  • P (1 bit): padding present at the end of the packet.
  • X (1 bit): exactly one header extension follows the fixed header.
  • CC (4 bits): the number of CSRC identifiers. At most 15 can be identified.
  • M (1 bit): a marker whose meaning is defined by a profile.
  • PT (7 bits): the payload type, which identifies the payload format.
  • sequence number (16 bits): increases by one per packet, with a random initial value, so receivers can detect loss and restore order.
  • timestamp (32 bits): the sampling instant of the first octet, with a random initial value. The clock frequency depends on the payload format.
  • SSRC (32 bits): the synchronization source identifier.

As an example, for fixed-rate audio the timestamp clock would likely increment by one per sampling period, so a block covering 160 sampling periods increases the timestamp by 160.

Profiles may tailor the header, and one optional extension mechanism exists for experiments. The extension begins with 16 bits defined by the profile and a 16-bit length counting 32-bit words. RFC 1889 defines no extensions itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a label on every piece of the video: which piece number it is, when it was recorded, what kind of data is inside, and who sent it.

sections.title: RTCP: Reports, Names and Rate Control
sections.content:
RTCP sends control packets periodically to all participants, using the same distribution mechanism as the data. It performs four functions: feedback on the quality of data distribution, carrying a persistent identifier called the CNAME, controlling the sending rate so RTP scales, and optionally conveying minimal session control information. The first three are mandatory for IP multicast.

There are five packet types: SR (sender report, 200), RR (receiver report, 201), SDES (source description, 202), BYE (203) and APP (204). They are sent together in a compound packet that must begin with an SR or RR and include an SDES packet with a CNAME. A report block has fields such as fraction lost, cumulative number of packets lost, extended highest sequence number received and interarrival jitter. SR packets also carry an NTP timestamp, an RTP timestamp, and packet and octet counts, which let a source compute round-trip delay.

To keep control traffic from growing with the number of participants, RTCP bandwidth is suggested to be fixed at 5% of session bandwidth. Senders are collectively given at least 1/4 of it, the calculated interval has a minimum of 5 seconds, and it is randomized over 0.5 to 1.5 times the calculated value.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the call sometimes whispers a quick note to the group saying how clear the sound was and who they are. The notes are kept short so they do not drown out the conversation.

sections.title: SSRC Collisions, Security and Transport
sections.content:
Because SSRC identifiers are random, two sources could pick the same one. All implementations MUST be prepared to detect collisions. A source that finds another using its identifier MUST send an RTCP BYE for the old one and choose another. The same uniqueness lets implementations detect loops created by mixers or translators.

For confidentiality, the RFC defines encryption of RTP and RTCP together as a unit, with a random 32-bit prefix for RTCP. The default algorithm is DES in CBC mode. Authentication and message integrity are not defined, since they would need a key management infrastructure, and are expected to come from lower layers.

Over UDP, RTP uses an even port number and RTCP uses the next higher odd port. The RFC also warns that high-bandwidth services such as video can degrade other network services, so implementors should limit accidental bandwidth use.
sections.plainLanguage: If two people pick the same name tag, one must say goodbye and pick a new one. For secrecy, the whole message is locked in a box before sending.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Padding octets at the end are not payload.

fields.name: X
fields.desc: One header extension follows the fixed header.

fields.name: CC
fields.desc: Number of CSRC identifiers that follow.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Profile-defined marker, such as a frame boundary.

fields.name: PT
fields.desc: Payload type: identifies the payload format.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: Increments by one for each RTP data packet sent.

fields.name: Timestamp
fields.desc: Sampling instant of the first octet of the payload.

items.label: SR
items.desc: Sender report: transmission and reception statistics from active senders.

items.label: RR
items.desc: Receiver report: reception statistics from participants that are not active senders.

items.label: SDES
items.desc: Source description items, including the CNAME.
